chapter_theme: The Renunciation sarukkam continues with King Payapati announcing to the young princes that he has resolved to leave, his queens and ministers taking up austerity with him, his crown cast into the milk sea by the gods, the thousand kings laying down theirs, the sons' grief and its consolation, and the king's arming himself with the five vows, virtues and disciplines against karma.

cast.role: King Payapati of Suramai land, who renounces and gives the realm to his sons
the young princes, the king's sons and kin, as a group
the conch-coloured prince, taken to be Vijayan
the discus-bearing prince with Fortune on his chest, taken to be Tivittan
the gods who carry off the crown
the thousand kings who take off their crowns with the king
the sages who console the princes

2090.reading: The poet recalls the king who once ruled while kings bowed at his feet, the sounds of royal drums, and a younger brother, and then turns to the manner of the chastity of a woman who enters the wedding.
2090.nuance: The verse is broken: the line about the 'chastity of her who enters the bridal home' (line 4) has no stated link to the king in lines 1 to 3, and the younger brother is not named, so the verse is read only as a closing view of the old royal state before the renunciation begins.

2091.reading: The king tells his hearers that such is her nature and that they should not cherish her as wealth, for once the people uphold the protector of living beings, they should look to their own duty.
2091.nuance: 'She' (இவள், அவள்) is not named here; she may be royal fortune or the land, but the verse does not say, so the reading keeps the warning against loving her as property and nothing more.

claims.claim: what is by nature fleeting is not to be cherished as one's own wealth

2092.reading: The king tells the garlanded ones that the guarding of the sea-fenced land, with its spear-bearing warriors, now rests with them, and that he has begun to set his own rule, so they should look to the time.
2092.nuance: The sense of line 3 (யானினி எனக்கு அரசாக்கல் உற்றனன்) is not fixed: it may mean he has turned to rule himself, or has taken up some other sovereignty, and the verse leaves it open.
2092.event: The king hands over the guardianship of the land to the young princes and announces his own turn to another rule.

2093.reading: The king says that the days left to him with them are few and their own days many, so the learned should put away grief, for he has resolved today.
2093.event: Payapati tells his people he has resolved to leave.

claims.claim: one's remaining span is short and the time to act is now

2094.reading: The young princes bow and ask what fault they have committed against their lord, and he, already like a stranger to them, answers that they have done nothing wrong.
2094.event: The young princes ask what fault they have done; the king answers that it is nothing they did.

2095.reading: He calls the queens, dear as nectar, and asks why their long eyes weep; they take up austerity before the king.
2095.event: The king asks the queens why they weep; they take up the vow before him.

2096.reading: The ministers who had practised austerity, trembling at the disease of birth, now by the grace of the king-of-kings throw off the great burden they bore.
2096.event: The ministers, who have been practising austerity, put down the burden of the body by the king's grace.

claims.claim: austerity is practised in dread of the disease of rebirth

2097.reading: The lord of the land of Suramai, with resolution, bathes in water from the milk sea and takes off his many jewelled ornaments for the great ascetics.
2097.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are tangled (the gods' part in bringing the milk-sea water and the crown's place); only the bath and the taking off of ornaments are firm.
2097.event: Payapati bathes and puts off his ornaments in the presence of the ascetics.

2098.reading: The king gives up his hard-won crown, and the gods take the gem-clustered crown away and cast it into the milk sea as if it were a great crown of their own sea.
2098.nuance: The throwing of the king's crown into the sea of the gods turns a loss of rank into an offering; the verse itself does not say who sees this.
2098.event: Payapati renounces the crown; the gods carry it off and cast it into the milk sea.

2099.reading: The king gives the drum-loud army and the sea-ringed earth to his sons and goes, and a thousand kings with their king-of-kings take their fragrant crowns off and put them aside.
2099.event: Payapati gives the kingdom to his sons and a thousand kings follow him in taking off their crowns.

claims.claim: a king's rule is to be laid aside and the realm passed on when he turns to renunciation

2100.reading: The crowns, bracelets, pearl necklaces, earrings and ornaments thrown off shine like blazing fires where they lie.
2100.event: The kings throw away their crowns and jewels.

2101.reading: As the blazing gem crown comes down from the lord's head, the two sons, conch-coloured Vijayan and discus-chested Tivittan, cry out like the sea of coiled conches.
2101.nuance: The two are identified only by epithets (the conch-coloured one and the discus-bearer with Fortune on his chest); the names are the reader's inference from the story.
2101.event: Vijayan and Tivittan wail as their father's crown falls.

2102.reading: Though they are dear to him, his love has gone beyond reach and the lord has become one with no tie to them, so they melt like wax in a bellows-fire and their flower eyes fill with water.
2102.event: The princes melt in grief at the lord's detachment.

claims.claim: love for dear ones is let go entirely by the one who renounces

2103.reading: The princes lament that the lord who once drew them to his fragrant chest while kings bowed has become like a stranger, and that this is cruel and great.
2103.nuance: The speaker is the two princes together as a pair (the cast has no id for a pair), so the speaker is given as the one named elsewhere, Tivittan, which is only a convenience.
2103.event: The princes complain that their lord has turned away from them.

2104.reading: They ask who now will take the garland from his chest and mount to him, and who will honour them as their own in the way he did, and so they depart in grief with flowered crowns.

2105.reading: The sage tells the young princes that the might which, by unmoving valour, bends the world was given up today by the lord, so there is nothing for them to grieve.
2105.nuance: The line 1 phrase (நின்றிலா நிலைமையில் நீங்கி) is hard; the reading keeps only that the consolation turns on the king's act being a higher victory.
2105.event: The sage consoles the young princes.

claims.claim: the valour that conquers the world is a lesser thing than the king's renunciation

2106.reading: The proud princes bow to the sages and say that if this is the grace of the lord, then their quarrelsome prattle was foolish, neither his quality nor his intent.
2106.event: The princes accept the king's act and bow.

2107.reading: The princes resolve not to grieve the lord's mind further by their talk, bow low with blazing crowns and go back to the rich city.
2107.event: The princes return to the capital.

2108.reading: The warrior returns to the king and says it is not fitting to serve here, since the lord had held the broad wealth and the sea-ringed earth as dust underfoot, and bows to the spear-bearer.
2108.nuance: The returning figure and the 'spear-bearer' (வேற்படை வீரன்) are not named in the verse.
2108.event: A warrior worships the spear-bearing lord and goes back.

claims.claim: wealth and the whole earth are to be counted as dust by the one who renounces

2109.reading: The lord lays down the spear and enters the ascetic's kingdom of heroic austerity, looks with the eye of the sages of the scripture, and stations five great captains of the vow-army to hold back the karma that advances.
2109.event: Payapati lays down his spear and sets five vows as guards against incoming karma.

claims.claim: the five great vows ward off the karma that is coming in

2110.reading: The lord arrays the army of virtues, the army of disciplines in eighteen thousand and the aids as instruments, and sets the maiden called mind firmly in their keeping.
2110.nuance: Line 3 (துணைப்படை பிறர்க்குச் செய்யும் துருநயத் தளவு நீக்கி) is obscure; the counts of the virtue-army are read as the poet's figures, not checked.
2110.event: Payapati arms himself with virtues and disciplines and guards the mind.

claims.claim: the mind is to be held firm by the army of virtues and disciplines

links.note: 2093 has the king say his own days are few and he has resolved today; Kural 342 says renounce while there is time.
links.teaches: The Kural's urgency to renounce in time becomes, in the epic, a king's own reckoning of his remaining days against those of his people.

gains.a: The king's haste gets a rule from outside the story: the time to renounce is limited and it is wiser to act before it runs out.
gains.b: The couplet gains a person who is at once a ruler and a father, whose leaving has to be explained to those he leaves.

links.note: In 2094 the princes ask what fault they have done; in 2106 they call their quarrelsome prattle foolish and bow to the lord's grace.
links.teaches: The sons' first grief as a charge against themselves turns, after the sages' consolation, into acceptance of the king's act as grace.

links.note: 2096 has the ministers put down the heavy burden they bore through the disease of birth; Kural 345 says that for those set on cutting off births even the body is excess.
links.teaches: The burden of the body in the epic is lifted by a king's grace, whereas the couplet lays it on the renouncer's own will.

gains.a: The ministers' burden gets a stated reason, that the body itself is surplus when one wants to end births.
gains.b: The couplet gains a scene of a king's court letting go together, where the renouncer is no lone figure.

links.note: 2098 has gods carry the king's crown and cast it into the milk sea; Cintamani 3035 has gods lift the tray with Civakan's hair and let it fall into the milk sea.
links.teaches: Both Jain epics end a royal career with the same act, gods taking the shed sign of rank to the milk sea, so the image reads as a convention for a king's completed renunciation.

links.note: 2099 has a king give army and earth to his sons and put off his crown by choice; Naladiyar 21 says even kings under umbrellas have been carried off as dead.
links.teaches: The same fall of a king from rank that Naladiyar reads as death's work is here done by the king's own hand while alive.

gains.a: The king's laying aside of the crown gets the contrast of what happens to kings who wait to be taken by death.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king who is not carried off but leaves before he must.

links.note: 2099 has the king leave wealth, army and earth to his sons; Tirumanthiram 168 says join the true wealth before the elephants, chariots and wealth pass to others.
links.teaches: Both tell a king to leave his wealth while he lives, but the epic hands it to sons and takes no god, while Tirumular names the one to join.

gains.a: The king's giving of the realm to his sons gets a rival reading, in which the wealth should be exchanged for the lord, not left to heirs.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram verse gains a case where the same urging is met without a god, by a vow and a handing over to the next generation.

links.note: 2101 shows the princes wailing as the crown falls from the lord; Kural 347 says griefs hold those who hold attachment.
links.teaches: The princes' grief shows the couplet's point from the other side: the renouncer is free while those who still cling to him suffer.

gains.a: The princes' sorrow is named as the cost of their own attachment, not only of his act.
gains.b: The couplet gains persons whose grief arises from clinging to another renouncer, not to things.

links.note: 2109 posts five great captains of the vow-army against incoming karma; Kural 343 says the domain of the five must be crushed and all desire let go.
links.teaches: The epic's five are vows that hold karma back, not the five senses of the couplet, so the same number is taken from two different disciplines.

gains.a: The five vows gain the older frame of crushing the five senses, which shows what they guard against.
gains.b: The couplet gains a Jain version in which the defence is a set of vows and an army, not a single act of crushing.

source_issues: Verses 2090 to 2092 are only partly clear: the 'her' of 2090 and 2091 and the sense of 2092 line 3 cannot be fixed, so they are marked uncertain.
2109 and 2110 print as eight half-lines in the build and are repaired to four lines; 2110 line 3 is obscure.
The speaker of the consolation in 2105 is inferred as the sages; the sons' names are inferred from epithets in 2101.
